title: The Sea That Was Switched Off

concept.logline: The fourth-largest lake on Earth vanished in one lifetime. Not to a drought, but to a decision about where its rivers should go. And one dike shows part of it can be switched back on.
concept.central_question: How do you lose a sea, and once it is gone, can you get it back?
concept.conflict: Cotton against a sea: two rivers could feed the fields or the Aral, not both.
concept.discovery: The sea was not lost to nature but to plumbing, and plumbing can be partly reversed: a 13 km dike brought the northern sea and its fish back.
concept.unanswered: Whether Soviet planners expected to lose the sea is still disputed; whether the northern recovery can last is uncertain.
concept.consequences: A fishing economy gone, a new salt desert, dust that residents blame for illness.
concept.implications: Water is allocated, not just available: the same choice faces every river basin that is over-drawn.
concept.structure_note: a mystery opened on the ships in the sand, solved by following the water upstream, turned by the dike
concept.visual_concept: Measured geography: real outlines and real terrain carry the story; the water is the accent; evidence is held still
concept.footage_strategy: Archive photographs of Moynaq and the fleet where a licence allows (on the pod); here every place is a measured map or a labelled drawing

act_titles.world: A sea with no way out
act_titles.consequences: What the sea took with it

scenes.narration: In the desert of western Uzbekistan, there is a town with a harbour, and fishing boats rusting in the sand.
scenes.graphic: Hero: ship | SHIPS IN THE SAND | Moynaq · Uzbekistan | the old harbour | fx: dust | camera: still

scenes.narration: The nearest water is now about a hundred kilometres away. Some say more.
scenes.graphic: BigNumber: 100 km | ship | to the nearest water | Moynaq, Uzbekistan | badge: estimate

scenes.narration: Because this town was a port, on what was once the fourth largest lake on Earth.
scenes.graphic: Pinmap: Moynaq | Once a port | atlas | marker: the old shore

scenes.narration: So how do you lose a sea? And once it is gone, can you get it back?
scenes.graphic: Title3d: LOSING A SEA | The Aral Sea · 1960 to today

scenes.narration: The Aral Sea sits on the border of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, in the heart of Central Asia.
scenes.graphic: Pinmap: Aral Sea | The Aral Sea | atlas

scenes.narration: It has no way out to the ocean. Two rivers fill it, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, and the sun takes the water away.
scenes.graphic: Flowchart: Mountain snow → Two rivers → Aral Sea → Evaporation | A sea with no outlet

scenes.narration: As long as the rivers brought in what the sun took, the sea held its size. In 1960, it covered about 68,000 square kilometres.
scenes.graphic: BigNumber: 68,000 km² | steamer | the Aral Sea in 1960 | Fourth-largest lake on Earth

scenes.narration: Then, from the 1960s, the Soviet Union began taking that river water for something else.
scenes.graphic: Hero: tractor | THE PLAN | Soviet Union · 1960s | irrigation | style: box | camera: push

scenes.narration: The plan was cotton. Canals carried the rivers out into the desert to water the fields.
scenes.graphic: Flowchart: River → Canal → Cotton field → Export | Where the water went

scenes.narration: According to one account, the water taken from the rivers doubled between 1960 and 1980, and cotton production nearly doubled with it.
scenes.graphic: BigNumber: ×2 | cotton | water taken from the rivers, 1960 to 1980 | One account | badge: reported

scenes.narration: Some estimates say only a fifth to a quarter of that water ever reached the crops.
scenes.graphic: Slice: 25% | water | at most reached the crops | badge: estimate

scenes.narration: And the sea began to fall. According to the geographer Philip Micklin's figures, the southern sea's surface dropped from 53.4 metres above sea level in 1960 to 26.5 by 2009.
scenes.graphic: Trend: 1960 53.4, 2009 26.5 | Water level of the South Aral, metres | water | src: P. Micklin

scenes.narration: In the late 1980s, it broke in two: a small sea in the north, a large one in the south.
scenes.graphic: Pinmap: North Aral Sea | The sea splits | atlas | marker: late 1980s

scenes.narration: Put the old shoreline over today's, and the scale of it is hard to take in.
scenes.graphic: Shrink: Aral Sea | 1960 -> today | The sea that left | pins: Moynaq, Aralsk

scenes.narration: Measured from public map outlines, about 67,500 square kilometres of water is down to around 6,800. NASA puts the loss at roughly ninety percent.
scenes.graphic: Bars3d: 1960 67,500, Today 6,800 | Water, square kilometres | km²

scenes.narration: In 2014, NASA's satellites showed the eastern half of the southern sea completely dry, for the first time in modern history.
scenes.graphic: Calendar: AUG 2014 | The eastern basin runs dry

scenes.narration: What it left behind has a name: the Aralkum, often called the youngest desert in the world.
scenes.graphic: Terrain3d: Aral Sea | The Aralkum | 520 km | pins: Moynaq, Aralsk

scenes.narration: So the sea was not lost to a drought. It was lost to plumbing, to choices, repeated every season, about where the rivers should go.
scenes.graphic: Opener: water | Not a drought. *Plumbing.* | The turn

scenes.narration: Researchers measured the water getting saltier as it shrank: about ten grams of salt per litre in 1947, and about ninety by 2002. The ocean is around thirty-five.
scenes.graphic: Stack: bars | 1947 10, 2002 90, Ocean 35 | Salt, grams per litre | src: Univ. of Marburg

scenes.narration: Then the dust. Researchers say the storms lift salt and farm chemicals off the old seabed, and one study found the dust nearly doubled between 1984 and 2015.
scenes.graphic: Explode: Dust storm | Salt, Fertiliser residue, Pesticide residue, Sand | What the wind lifts

scenes.narration: People here have long blamed that dust for illness. The medical evidence is still debated.
scenes.graphic: Linkmap: The dust | Lungs: blamed; Eyes: blamed; Children: blamed; Water: blamed | What residents blame | badge: disputed

scenes.narration: The sea had fed a whole industry. In 1957, according to local accounts, its fishermen landed about 48,000 tonnes of fish.
scenes.graphic: Hero: steamer | THE CATCH | 1957 · 48,000 tonnes | local accounts | style: disc | badge: reported

scenes.narration: Estimates of how many people worked in those fisheries run from thirty thousand to sixty thousand.
scenes.graphic: Table: Estimate, People | Lowest, 30,000; Often cited, 40,000; Highest, 60,000 | Fishery jobs: the estimates | local histories | badge: disputed

scenes.narration: By one account, the cannery in Moynaq ended up processing fish brought in from the Baltic and the Pacific, until it closed around 1990.
scenes.graphic: Arrows: Latvia → Moynaq (Baltic fish) | Fish from far away | badge: reported

scenes.narration: Whether Soviet planners expected to lose the sea is still argued over. What it cost the people on its shore is not.
scenes.graphic: Hero: documents | WHO KNEW? | Soviet planners · 1960s | still debated | style: box | badge: disputed | camera: still

scenes.narration: But if the sea was lost to plumbing, could plumbing bring some of it back?
scenes.graphic: Morph: drop → circle → drop | Can it come back?

scenes.narration: In 2005, Kazakhstan finished a dike about thirteen kilometres long, built with the World Bank's help, to hold the river in the small northern sea.
scenes.graphic: Pinmap: Kok-Aral | The Kok-Aral dike | atlas | marker: the dike, 2005

scenes.narration: The northern sea rose. By 2008, according to researchers' figures, it stood at about 42 metres, while the south kept falling.
scenes.graphic: Bars3d: 1960 53.4, North 2008 42, South 2009 26.5 | Water level, metres above sea level | m

scenes.narration: And the fish came back. Kazakhstan's fisheries institute reports the catch grew from 695 tonnes in 2005 to 5,595 in 2014.
scenes.graphic: Trend: 2005 695, 2014 5,595 | North Aral fish catch, tonnes | fish | src: Kazakh fisheries institute via Eurasianet

scenes.narration: It is fragile. A 2026 report says the catch fell by half in 2025, from about 7,800 tonnes to 3,900, and officials now plan to raise the dike and the sea to 44 metres.
scenes.graphic: Table: Year, Catch (tonnes) | 2014, 5,595; Before 2025, 7,800; 2025, 3,900 | Up, then down | Kazakh data via Eurasianet, Global Voices | highlight: 3

scenes.narration: The southern sea has no such dike. It is still drying.
scenes.graphic: Shrink: Aral Sea | 1960 -> today | Still drying | pins: Moynaq

scenes.narration: So how do you lose a sea? The evidence suggests not with a drought, but with a decision. And the north shows that some decisions can be taken back.
scenes.graphic: Endcard: The Sea That Was Switched Off | Some decisions can be taken back | Sources: NASA · World Bank · Eurasianet · Natural Earth
